for (t in 1:seconds) {

                       prob = c(lambda_l,

    y_l[t] <- split[1]
    y_diff[t] <- split[2]
  }
}

but I'm unable to figure out how to code this clearly in Nimble. Would a user-defined function be useful here?

Thanks so much!
Meridith

Hi Meredith,

NIMBLE, along with JAGS and WinBUGS/OpenBUGS, uses a declarative model language.  That mean none of them will support the if-then structure you have or the re-use of split in the style of iterative (typical) programming. In other words, you can't re-use split for each t, because once it is declared it is part of the graph as declared, so you will need to index it by t.  Also model declarations need indexing. It is also not clear if you are trying to have a variable follow a multinomial (dmultinom) or to draw from a multinomial (rmultinom) in a nimbleFunction outside of a model, because it is not typical for an "r" function to appear in model code.  So, I can't really tell what you're trying to do.  If you are trying to write model code, and if I guess at your intention, it might be something like this:

nimbleCode({
for(t in 1:seconds) {
  split[t, 1:2] ~ dmultinom(size = y[t],
                                 prob = c(lambda_l,
                                               lambda_diff))
  y_l[t] <- (state[t] == 0) * y[t] + (state[t] != 0) * split[t, 1]
  y_diff[t] <- (state[t] != 0) * split[t, 2]
})

HTH
-Perry

messages.subject: MICAR and MPCAR models on Nimble
messages.subject_clean: MICAR and MPCAR models on Nimble
messages.body_plain:
For those interested in multivariate CAR modeling on Nimble:
as you may be aware Nimble does not currently have the equivalent to the mv.car distribution
which is available on Win/OpenBUGS. This distribution is an implementation of the multivariate ICAR
(MICAR), and it is the only MCAR distribution so far available.

On Nimble, the univariate ICAR and PCAR models are available (as in BUGS) . The linear model of coregionalisation (LMC)
allows the construction of MCAR models from combinations of univariate ICAR and PCAR distributions. As Nimble allows the
use of Cholesky decomposition it is possible to hand code both the MICAR and MPCAR models directly.

This has now been done and benchmark tests demonstrate that even without the conjugate Wishart sampling in the mv.car in BUGS ,
the Nimble implimentation of MICAR (the equivalent to mv.car) is marginally faster in execution, for the same data, than mv.car.
One major advantage of the the Nimble implementation of LMC is that the MPCAR can also be computed and so individual spatial correlation parameters can be estimated for each disease, as well as cross correlations. The MPCAR is not available on Win/OpenBUGS.

Code for both models for the Georgia county level 3 disease example is attached here

There is also a new dedicated GitHub repository for Nimble Bayesian Disease Mapping  code here:

https://github.com/Andrew9Lawson/Bayesian_DM_Nimble_code

Thanks also to Chris Paciorek for fixing bugs in the original Nimble code.

best wishes

hi Jose, in your RW_constrained, it should look like this (i.e., only have the [1] indexing when you use current_w, not when it is created.

        current_w <- target_vals
        if(abs(model[[constraintNode]] - current_w[1]) > 1e-6) print('Looks like the constraint is being violated\n')

The NIMBLE compiler will create current_w as a vector and then in the next line, you use the first element.

That will solve the particular error. However, there is a bigger issue here - 'constraintNode' is 'C' in your model, and that is a 3-d array.
But you are comparing to an individual element of 'y.full', which is a scalar.  I think you probably need to have the constraintNode
for each element of 'y.full' be the corresponding element of 'C'.

Chris

Vincent, thanks for your interest and use of NIMBLE.  I'm happy to hear about your plans for incorporating NIMBLE into your own R package(s).  I've done some work along the same lines, so let me try to provide some guidance for you.

But first, one question.  In your initial post, you said you're trying to register a NIMBLE distribution from *within a package function*.  It might complicate things if your custom distribution(s) need to be defined *inside package function(s)*.  So, is it the case that (1) your custom distribution(s) are dynamic, that is, they depend on the argument(s) to package function(s)?  Or, (2) your distribution(s) are static, and fully known in advance, and thus could be defined inside your package, and subsequently be used inside your package function(s)?

Assuming (2) is the case, which would be simpler, then, I would suggest the following:

In your package NAMESPACE file, make sure (a) to import the nimble package, and (b) to export your custom distribution.  That is, include the lines:

import(nimble)
export(dtvgeom)

Heads up, you may also need to import the methods package:

import(methods)

In your package DESCRIPTION file, explicitly have your package "depend" on nimble.  That is, include the line, e.g.:

Depends: R (>= 3.6.1),nimble

Then, in your package R source files, (e.g., yourPackage / R / foo.R), include the definition of your custom distribution, making sure to export it.  So, that would look something like:

#' Description of your distribution
#' ....
#' @export
dtvgeom <- nimbleFunction(
  run = function(...) {
    ...
  }, check = FALSE
)

Including the "check = FALSE" will avoid warnings, in some cases.  It's safe to include that, if you're entirely confident the definition of your custom distribution is correct.

Then, you'll be able to use the dtvgeom distribution inside your other package functions.

Please let us know if anything here is unclear, and/or how it works for you.

Cheers!  Keep in touch!
Daniel

assess the relative importance of predictor variables, following the
modelling structure suggested by Kuo and Mallick 1998. The WinBUGS
results of the indicator variables make ecological sense, while Nimble
doesn't.

I was wondering why the inclusion of indicator variables should yield
such drastically different results between WinBUGS and Nimble.

I would greatly appreciate any insights and pointers.

messages.subject: Can some vector elements be stochastic and others deterministic in NIMBLE?
messages.subject_clean: Can some vector elements be stochastic and others deterministic in NIMBLE?
messages.body_plain:
Hi all,

A nice trick in JAGS allows to users to feed parameter vectors as data with NA in the indices of parameters you want to sample, and fixed values for parameters you don't want to sample. This comes in handy, for example, when considering multiple random effects in multiple regression. If I have a vector of standard deviations for the random effects for each regression coefficient, i can fix the values to be 0 for the indices of parameters I don't want random effects on, and NAs in the indices of the parameters that I do want random effects on. This is super helpful because it allows you to tell the model which parameters should have random effects and which shouldn't -- no need to make a separate model file for every scenario. Is this possible to do in NIMBLE as well?

One other question, I saw this in the docs:
> 1. The appearance of the same node on the left-hand side of both a <- and a ∼ declaration (used in WinBUGS for data assignment for the value of a stochastic node).
Does that mean I can't assign some elements in a vector (or matrix) with <- and sample others stochastically?

Thanks very much for any insight/help!

- Vincent

messages.subject_clean: Can some vector elements be stochastic and others deterministic in NIMBLE?
messages.body_plain:
Hi Vincent,

Thanks for the questions.  They touch on a bunch of issues.

Yes, some elements of a non-scalar variable can be deterministic (created with "<-") while others can be stochastic (created with "~").

If your model is called m, you can explore model-querying features to see this.  E.g. m$getNodeNames(stochOnly = TRUE) or m$getNodeNames(determOnly = TRUE).

You can also have some stochastic nodes in a variable that are data and others that are not data.  This is distinct from deterministic vs. not deterministic.  Yes, nodes for which "data" is provided as NA will not be data but will instead be sampled, similar to what JAGS does.  You can explore these aspects of a model with, e.g., m$getNodeNames(dataOnly = TRUE) or m$getNodeNames(includeData = FALSE).

The prohibition on declaring a node with both "<-" and "~" is for a node, not for a different nodes in the same variable.
x[1] <- 2
x[2] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
is fine but
x[1] <- 2
x[1] ~ dnorm(0, 1)
is not allowed.

Finally, I believe the trick you are referring to, writing multiple random effects in a model and then turning some off in effect by setting their standard deviation to zero, leads to inefficient sampling (in nimble or jags).  That occurs because the MCMC does not see the situation and will still attempt to update every random effect on every iteration even though no value other than 0 (or whatever the mean is) will ever be accepted.  NIMBLE provides model-definition-time if-then-else so that you can turn model components on and off when you build the model, which means they won't exist and won't be sampled.  It can be a little cumbersome and we'd love to have someone write a more sophisticated system, but it is there and saves you from having many different model files.  You can learn more about that in the user manual or ask further questions if it's not clear.

-Perry

messages.body_plain:
It looks like you want Q*u[i] to be the standard deviation.  In JAGS, you create tau = precision = 1/(Q*u[i])^2.  In nimble it looks like you are using Q*u[i] and expecting it to be standard deviation.

nimble uses the same default parameterization as BUGS/JAGS, not R.  It does extend BUGS/JAGS by supporting alternative parameterizations via named parameters. Therefore the models you've used are not the same.  In nimble you are saying precision = Q*u[i].  It looks like what you intend is

M[i] ~ dnorm(mu[i], sd = Q*u[i])

Distributions and parameterizations are described in the nimble User Manual available at r-nimble.org <http://r-nimble.org>.

-Perry
